cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide public awareness campaign teaching residents how to plan meals, store food properly, and use leftovers creatively.
2. Partner with grocery stores to create clearly labeled “imperfect produce” sections sold at a discount.
3. Establish a municipal composting program that collects food scraps from households and businesses.
4. Create a food waste audit requirement for large supermarkets and institutional kitchens to track and report disposal volumes.
5. Offer small grants to restaurants that implement waste-reduction practices such as smaller portions or reusable prep systems.
6. Develop a mobile app connecting residents with local restaurants and bakeries selling surplus food at reduced prices.
7. Set up neighborhood “community fridges” where people can share excess edible food safely.
8. Require city-permitted events to donate unserved food to local shelters or food banks.
9. Train food service workers in schools and hospitals on waste tracking and prevention techniques.
10. Introduce standardized date labeling guidance to help residents understand “best by,” “use by,” and “sell by” dates.
11. Provide tax incentives to food businesses that donate edible surplus food to nonprofit organizations.
12. Install food scrap drop-off bins at farmers markets, libraries, and community centers.
13. Support local farms in using food waste as animal feed where safe and legal.
14. Create a city-run food recovery network that coordinates volunteers to collect surplus food from businesses.
15. Encourage restaurants to offer flexible portion sizes and take-home containers by default.
16. Fund school gardens that teach students about food value, composting, and seasonality.
17. Host monthly repair-and-cook events where residents learn to use overripe produce and pantry staples.
18. Require new commercial developments to include space for food waste separation and compost storage.
19. Work with food banks to improve cold storage and logistics for receiving perishable donations.
20. Launch a “zero-waste restaurant” certification program with public recognition and marketing support.
21. Use city data to identify neighborhoods with high food waste and target them with tailored interventions.
22. Provide subsidized compost bins and worm farms to households and apartment buildings.
23. Encourage supermarkets to convert near-expiry foods into prepared meals, soups, or smoothies.
24. Create a food waste reduction toolkit for small businesses with simple checklists and staff training guides.
25. Integrate food waste education into existing sustainability and climate action programs.
26. Partner with universities to pilot technologies such as smart bins, anaerobic digestion, or waste-to-energy systems.
27. Require municipal contracts with caterers to include food waste prevention and donation clauses.
28. Develop a public dashboard showing city progress on food waste reduction, donation, and composting.
29. Train building managers in apartments and offices to set up shared food-sharing shelves and compost systems.
30. Support cultural and community organizations in hosting waste-free cooking demonstrations.
31. Incentivize grocery stores to donate unsold bakery, dairy, and prepared foods rather than discarding them.
32. Establish a city food policy council with a dedicated food waste reduction task force.
33. Create standardized signage for food donation, composting, and landfill bins across public facilities.
34. Run seasonal campaigns focused on preserving summer produce and using holiday leftovers.
35. Provide free or low-cost food safety training to nonprofits handling donated perishable food.
36. Encourage hotels and conference centers to track banquet overproduction and adjust purchasing accordingly.
37. Launch a school lunch waste reduction program with share tables for unopened food and composting for scraps.
38. Work with waste haulers to offer lower rates to businesses that separate food waste and reduce landfill disposal.
39. Create a directory of local services that accept food scraps for composting, animal feed, or bioenergy.
40. Encourage residents to adopt “first in, first out” kitchen habits by keeping older food visible and accessible.
41. Support food entrepreneurs who make products from surplus ingredients, such as jams, sauces, or dried snacks.
42. Add food waste reduction goals to the city’s climate action plan and annual sustainability reporting.
43. Host a yearly food waste challenge with prizes for households, schools, and businesses that reduce waste the most.
44. Install anaerobic digesters at wastewater treatment facilities to process collected food waste into energy.
45. Require city departments to prioritize reusable, redistributable, or compostable food systems in procurement.
46. Create multilingual food storage and waste-reduction guides tailored to the city’s diverse communities.
47. Partner with faith groups and community kitchens to collect and redistribute surplus event food.
48. Encourage grocery stores to reduce overstocking by using demand forecasting and smaller, more frequent deliveries.
49. Pilot a pay-as-you-throw program that charges residents based on landfill waste weight while offering free compost collection.
50. Recognize local leaders, businesses, and schools that achieve measurable food waste reduction through an annual awards program.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. A citywide “ugly produce” brand turns misshapen farm goods into affordable snack boxes sold at transit hubs.  
2. Smart bins in grocery stores weigh discarded food and print donation receipts for tax-credit eligible surplus.  
3. A mobile “rescue kitchen” truck converts restaurant surplus into free community meals within hours.  
4. Neighborhood “food libraries” let residents borrow pantry staples and return them with interest in homegrown produce.  
5. Schools host “leftover labs” where students transform cafeteria scraps into compost, recipes, and science projects.  
6. A municipal app matches households with surplus fruit trees to volunteers who harvest and share the bounty.  
7. Restaurants earn a “zero-waste star” rating by publishing weekly food-waste audits and reduction goals.  
8. A city-run fermentation hub helps residents turn surplus vegetables into shelf-stable sauces, pickles, and kimchi.  
9. Grocery stores create “mystery baskets” of near-expiry items discounted through a gamified loyalty program.  
10. Farmers markets install “seconds stalls” selling imperfect produce at tiered prices to canners, juicers, and charities.  
11. A “bread bank” collects day-old bakery goods and redistributes them through shelters, schools, and community fridges.  
12. Compostable packaging made from local crop residues labels food products with storage tips to extend freshness.  
13. A “food waste currency” rewards residents for diverting edible surplus, redeemable at local farms and cafes.  
14. City buses carry small refrigerated rescue pods that collect surplus food from small stores on their routes.  
15. A public “banquet of imperfection” festival celebrates meals cooked entirely from rescued ingredients.  
16. Hotels use AI portion forecasting to adjust breakfast buffets and donate untouched surplus to breakfast programs.  
17. A network of cold-storage lockers lets restaurants and grocers leave safe surplus food for scheduled nonprofit pickup.  
18. Community gardens dedicate beds to “waste-to-soil” demonstrations using food scraps from nearby apartments.  
19. A city ordinance requires event venues to publish food-surplus plans and donate catered leftovers within 24 hours.  
20. Local breweries partner with bakeries to turn stale bread into specialty beer and spent grains into crackers.  
21. A “last-hour marketplace” app aggregates same-day discounts from grocers, delis, and bakeries within walking distance.  
22. Public housing kitchens host weekly “cook-the-fridge” classes focused on using leftovers and wilting produce.  
23. A food-waste art program commissions murals and sculptures made from non-edible scraps to raise awareness.  
24. Libraries lend dehydrators, vacuum sealers, and canning kits so residents can preserve surplus at home.  
25. A “restaurant plate-size menu” lets diners choose smaller portions at lower prices to reduce plate waste.  
26. City vehicles powered by biogas from food waste display “powered by leftovers” messaging and collection schedules.  
27. A school curriculum ties math lessons to measuring cafeteria waste and designing reduction campaigns.  
28. A “food rescue relay” uses cyclists, seniors, and rideshare drivers to move surplus from stores to shelters quickly.  
29. Grocery stores place “eat first” shelves at eye level with recipe cards for items nearing best-by dates.  
30. A city-sponsored “waste-free wedding pledge” helps caterers plan donation and compost protocols for events.  
31. A network of community freezers maps real-time surplus food availability through open city data.  
32. Restaurants offer “doggy bags with a twist” by including compostable containers and a QR code for leftover recipes.  
33. A municipal “food waste hotline” connects businesses with emergency pickup volunteers when surplus appears.  
34. Urban farms accept fruit pits, peels, and trimmings to create pest-repellent mulches and animal-free soil amendments.  
35. A “rescue dinner series” invites chefs to compete using only ingredients that would have been discarded.  
36. Supermarkets train staff to “shop the back” and rotate perishables with color-coded freshness tags.  
37. A city grant program funds small restaurants to buy blast chillers for safely storing rescued meals.  
38. A “zero-waste food truck” demonstrates portable preservation techniques like pickling, drying, and flash freezing.  
39. Offices adopt “meeting meal match” policies so catered leftovers are claimed by employees or local shelters.  
40. A “food scrap pharmacy” collects citrus peels, herb stems, and coffee grounds for natural cleaners and beauty products.  
41. A city-run repair café teaches residents to fix small kitchen appliances that help prevent food spoilage.  
42. A “harvest swap” calendar coordinates backyard gardeners to exchange excess produce before it spoils.  
43. Local radio segments broadcast daily “surplus specials” from participating grocery stores and eateries.  
44. A food-waste audit challenge pairs businesses with university students to identify loss points in storage and purchasing.  
45. A “mystery soup day” at community centers turns donated vegetables into large-batch meals and frozen portions.  
46. City parks host composting stations with clear signage showing what becomes soil, biogas, or animal feed.  
47. A “no-waste lunchbox” campaign gives families reusable containers, shopping guides, and leftover-friendly recipes.  
48. A “food recovery ambassador” program trains residents to educate neighbors about date labels and safe storage.  
49. A city-sponsored “residuals market” sells value-added products like vegetable powder, bread crumbs, and fruit leather made from surplus.  
50. A “waste-to-wishes” holiday drive lets residents donate rescued groceries to fulfill meal requests from local families.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Conduct a citywide food-waste audit to identify the largest sources of waste in homes, stores, restaurants, and institutions.
2. Require supermarkets and large grocers to separate edible unsold food for donation or discounted resale.
3. Establish a chilled redistribution hub that collects, stores, and quickly routes surplus perishable food to charities.
4. Offer local tax incentives or fee reductions to restaurants that donate safe surplus meals.
5. Create a clear public campaign that explains the difference between “best before,” “sell by,” and “use by” dates.
6. Organize a gleaning network that connects volunteers with farms, gardens, and orchards to collect surplus produce.
7. Provide small grants to restaurants and caterers for training chefs in root-to-stem and nose-to-tail cooking.
8. Launch curbside food-scrap collection for households and small food businesses.
9. Install clearly labeled food-waste bins in markets, food courts, parks, and transit hubs.
10. Support a mobile app that alerts residents to discounted near-expiry food at nearby stores.
11. Ask large food businesses to publish simple annual food-waste amounts and reduction plans.
12. Create a tagging system that marks damaged or near-expiry food for rescue, discounting, composting, or animal feed based on its condition.
13. Add food-waste lessons to school curricula, covering meal planning, storage, and creative leftovers.
14. Encourage takeout restaurants to offer smaller default portions and reusable container options.
15. Encourage grocers to sell imperfect or oddly shaped produce at lower prices.
16. Train food-safety inspectors to advise businesses on safe donation, storage, and date-label practices.
17. Support community fridges with maintenance, cleaning protocols, and clear food-safety rules.
18. Develop anaerobic digestion capacity for inedible food scraps that cannot be rescued or composted locally.
19. Require city-funded events to include a food-waste prevention, donation, and composting plan.
20. Distribute simple kitchen kits with storage containers, freezer bags, and portion guides to households.
21. Require caterers working with the city to plan portions carefully and donate safe surplus food.
22. Encourage grocery stores to use dynamic pricing or shelf tags for items approaching their best-by dates.
23. Partner with food banks to improve their ability to receive and distribute perishable donations.
24. Offer free training for small retailers on managing near-expiry stock and reducing shrink.
25. Design calm, specific food-waste prompts that stand out without relying on louder messaging.
26. Simplify permits and loading-zone rules so food-rescue organizations can collect surplus food quickly.
27. Pilot pay-as-you-throw waste pricing

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside food-scrap collection program that sends organics to composting or anaerobic digestion.
2. Require grocery stores and restaurants to report food waste volumes and set annual reduction targets.
3. Create a digital marketplace connecting restaurants, grocers, and caterers with local food banks for same-day donations.
4. Fund a gleaning network that collects surplus produce from urban farms, community gardens, and backyard trees.
5. Introduce “ugly produce” discounts at supermarkets and farmers markets to normalize imperfect fruits and vegetables.
6. Provide small grants for restaurants to redesign menus around seasonal, whole-ingredient, and trim-friendly dishes.
7. Require municipal facilities, schools, and hospitals to conduct food waste audits and publish reduction plans.
8. Support community refrigerators where residents and businesses can leave safe, surplus food for neighbors.
9. Train food-service workers in inventory management, batch cooking, and proper storage to prevent spoilage.
10. Offer tax credits or fee reductions to businesses that donate edible food or compost food scraps.
11. Run a public awareness campaign on meal planning, storage tips, and “best before” versus “use by” dates.
12. Install clearly labeled food-waste bins in parks, transit hubs, and municipal buildings with signage in multiple languages.
13. Partner with schools to teach children about food waste through school gardens, cooking classes, and cafeteria audits.
14. Pilot a pay-as-you-throw pricing system that charges households less when they separate food waste from trash.
15. Establish a food recovery hub that aggregates surplus food from multiple small businesses for efficient redistribution.
16. Encourage grocery stores to sell smaller portions and imperfect bundles for single-person and small households.
17. Create a certification program for restaurants that meet food waste reduction, donation, and composting standards.
18. Use city data to identify neighborhoods with high food waste disposal and target them with education and collection services.
19. Support a tool-lending library for food preservation equipment such as dehydrators, vacuum sealers, and canning kits.
20. Host neighborhood cooking demonstrations that show how to use stale bread, vegetable scraps, and overripe fruit.
21. Require event organizers to submit food waste plans for festivals, markets, and large public gatherings.
22. Work with food banks to improve cold storage, refrigerated transport, and last-mile delivery for donated perishable food.
23. Provide city-owned refrigerated space for temporary food donation pop-ups after markets and festivals.
24. Develop a municipal procurement policy that favors vendors with verified food waste reduction practices.
25. Encourage hotels and conference centers to offer flexible catering portions and donate safe leftovers.
26. Launch a “last hour” program where bakeries, delis, and cafés discount items that would otherwise be discarded.
27. Create a network of composting sites at community gardens and farms to process local food scraps into soil amendments.
28. Partner with waste haulers to offer food waste tracking bins that help businesses measure and reduce disposal.
29. Fund a pilot for anaerobic digestion that converts food waste into biogas for city vehicles or facilities.
30. Train city inspectors and health officials to give clear guidance on safe food donation and handling.
31. Encourage grocery stores to use dynamic pricing that lowers costs as products approach their best-by dates.
32. Require new large residential developments to include space for separated food waste collection and compost storage.
33. Create a city-supported app that helps residents plan meals, track pantry items, and find local surplus food deals.
34. Establish a food waste hotline or online portal where residents can report spoiled bulk purchases or request pickup for surplus food.
35. Partner with local farms to safely collect and feed appropriate food scraps to livestock where regulations allow.
36. Support food cooperatives that buy directly from farmers and use whole-case purchasing to reduce unsold inventory.
37. Introduce a “no-waste menu” week featuring restaurants that use roots, stems, peels, and leftovers creatively.
38. Provide businesses with standardized date-labeling guidance to reduce confusion about food safety and freshness.
39. Create a volunteer food rescue team that can pick up small surplus donations from homes and small businesses.
40. Use city communications to celebrate residents, chefs, and businesses that achieve measurable food waste reductions.
41. Require caterers to ask clients about portion preferences and provide takeaway containers for uneaten event food.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Create a citywide “Food Rescue Rail” using electric cargo bikes to move surplus restaurant food to shelters within 30 minutes.  
2. Install smart bins in supermarkets that weigh discarded food and automatically donate equivalent funds to local food banks.  
3. Host monthly “Ugly Produce Festivals” celebrating misshapen fruits and vegetables with cooking demos, music, and discounts.  
4. Offer property-tax rebates to landlords who lease unused commercial kitchens to food-rescue startups.  
5. Build neighborhood “Community Fridges” powered by solar panels where residents and shops can leave edible surplus food.  
6. Train a team of “Food Waste Auditors” to help households, schools, and restaurants diagnose their waste patterns.  
7. Introduce a municipal app that gamifies saving food by awarding points redeemable for bus passes and local discounts.  
8. Turn expired-but-safe bakery goods into a branded city flour for community baking classes.  
9. Create a “Last Meal Kit” service that bundles near-expiry groceries into chef-designed dinner kits.  
10. Require all city events to submit food-waste prevention plans and donate leftovers.  
11. Establish a mobile “Soup Cycle” truck that converts surplus vegetables into fresh soups for school lunch programs.  
12. Launch a “Plate Passport” program encouraging diners to finish meals or request smaller portions for rewards.  
13. Partner with pet-food makers to safely convert meat trimmings and unsold seafood into local pet products.  
14. Set up anaerobic digesters at farmers’ markets to convert inedible scraps into biogas for market stalls.  
15. Fund “Zero-Waste Kitchen” microgrants for immigrant and refugee home cooks to teach preservation workshops.  
16. Place QR-coded recipe posters near grocery store produce sections using ingredients commonly thrown away.  
17. Create a city-supported “Surplus Subscription Box” where consumers receive discounted imperfect produce and near-date pantry items.  
18. Give restaurants a “Small Plate, Big Taste” certification for offering flexible portion sizes and takeaway containers.  
19. Use AI cameras in school cafeterias to track which menu items are wasted and redesign meals accordingly.  
20. Convert fruit peels and coffee grounds into city-branded cleaning products, compost, or bio-textiles through local makerspaces.  
21. Start a “Bread Bank” where bakeries donate day-old loaves to soup kitchens and community toasters.  
22. Create edible landscaping in public parks featuring berry bushes, herbs, and fruit trees with harvest-sharing guidelines.  
23. Offer free “Fridge Fitness” checkups for residents to learn optimal storage, freezing, and shelf organization.  
24. Introduce a “Waste-Free Lunch League” where schools compete to reduce cafeteria waste with real-time scoreboards.  
25. Let residents compost food scraps at community gardens in exchange for plots, seeds, or fresh produce.  
26. Create a “Midnight Market” selling discounted same-day restaurant meals and bakery items before closing.  
27. Provide tax incentives to grocery stores that create dedicated “Rescue Aisles” for near-expiry and imperfect goods.  
28. Deploy refrigerated lockers at transit hubs where residents can pick up rescued meals ordered through a city app.  
29. Train baristas to turn surplus milk into cheese, yogurt, or baked goods through micro-dairy partnerships.  
30. Create a “Food Waste Court” theater series where comedians and chefs judge absurd food-waste scenarios to educate residents.  
31. Require large catering companies to publish annual food-waste reports and donate surplus meals to registered nonprofits.  
32. Launch a “Holiday Rescue Hotline” where residents can schedule pickups of extra cooked food after celebrations.  
33. Build a city food-processing hub that turns seasonal gluts into frozen, dried, canned, or fermented products.  
34. Give households color-coded bins that separate edible surplus, compost, and inedible waste with simple guidance.  
35. Start a “Restaurant Leftover Lounge” pop-up where high-end kitchens reinvent surplus ingredients into tasting menus.  
36. Offer local breweries discounts on surplus bread and fruit to create small-batch beers and fermented drinks.  
37. Create a “Food Rescue Youth Corps” where students earn service credits by collecting, sorting, and redistributing surplus food.  
38. Install public dehydration stations near markets to preserve surplus herbs, tomatoes, and apples for food banks.  
39. Develop a “Date Label Decoder” campaign explaining best-before and use-by labels through street art and transit ads.  
40. Turn food-waste collection trucks into mobile classrooms with transparent bins and short educational broadcasts.  
41. Create a “Zero-Waste Catering Seal” for weddings and funerals that includes donation logistics and composting.  
42. Establish a city seed-to-table program that grows food in vacant lots and requires harvest-sharing agreements.  
43. Provide restaurants with compostable takeaway containers printed with storage and reheating instructions to reduce home leftovers waste.  
44. Launch a “Mystery Basket Challenge” where local chefs compete using only rescued ingredients.  
45. Create a neighborhood “Preservation Library” where residents borrow fermentation crocks, dehydrators, and canning kits.  
46. Introduce pay-as-you-throw food-waste pricing with rebates for households that prove lower waste through smart bins.  
47. Partner with hotels to rescue buffet leftovers safely and transform them into staff meals or shelter donations.  
48. Build an open-data dashboard mapping food waste by district, business type, and season to guide targeted interventions.  
49. Fund a “Food Waste Lab” that tests insect farming, mushroom cultivation, or mycelium packaging using urban food scraps.  
50. Establish an annual “City Feast” where a free public meal is cooked entirely from rescued food and hosted in the town square.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Two strangers wake up in a locked bedroom with no memory of the night before and must decide whether to trust each other before a timer expires.
2. A job interview in an empty office turns sinister when the interviewer asks about a crime the candidate has not confessed to yet.
3. Two siblings sorting their late parent’s bedroom find a hidden letter that changes who they think deserved the house.
4. A couple rehearsing their breakup accidentally reveals the true fear that keeps them from leaving each other.
5. An insomniac and a burglar trapped together during a blackout negotiate a truce until dawn.
6. Two friends reviewing a selfie video realize one of them has been replaced by a double only the camera can see.
7. A landlord showing a room to a tenant discovers the tenant knows every secret the previous occupant left behind.
8. Two rival coworkers stuck in a conference room confess to sabotaging each other before the company laptop shuts down.
9. A couple assembling a crib argue about parenthood until they hear a knock from inside the wardrobe.
10. Two actors waiting for an audition begin performing each other’s private memories as if they were scripted scenes.
11. A detective interrogates a suspect in a hotel room until the suspect proves the detective has been asleep during the crime.
12. Two ex-lovers dividing their books accidentally recreate the argument that ended their relationship.
13. A sleepwalker enters a stranger’s room and convinces the occupant they are both caught in the same dream.
14. Two neighbors stuck in a soundproofed room must use gestures to stop a hidden timer before it reaches zero.
15. A bride and a wedding photographer hide in a bathroom while someone searches outside, each protecting a different secret.
16. Two cleaners hired for the same apartment realize they have been paid to erase evidence of each other’s existence.
17. A mother and son listening to old cassette tapes discover recordings that contradict the story of their family.
18. Two coworkers locked in a meeting room by their company’s AI must choose who will take the blame for missing data.
19. A blind date becomes uncanny when both people insist they have met in this exact room before.
20. Two friends practicing a marriage proposal reveal that they are both secretly in love with someone else.
21. A tenant tries to prove the room is haunted while the landlord seems more afraid of what the tenant knows.
22. Two applicants for the same apartment try to sabotage each other’s viewing without leaving the room.
23. A couple filming a farewell message to their future selves discovers one of them has already changed the recording.
24. Two strangers receive identical texts warning that the other person is dangerous, but neither can leave the room.
25. A therapist and patient swap roles for five minutes and the experiment becomes dangerously real.
26. Two friends hiding from a party in a bedroom discover the room belongs to someone who does not exist.
27. A painter and a model argue over whether the portrait is revealing the truth or creating it.
28. Two delivery drivers arrive at the same locked room with packages addressed to each other.
29. A couple rehearsing a eulogy keeps breaking down because each blames the other for the death.
30. Two strangers in a hotel room discover a hidden camera that has been recording them for years.
31. A tutor and student struggle through a lesson until the tutor admits the lesson is a confession.
32. Two siblings recording a birthday message for their estranged father expose a new family resentment with every take.
33. A couple playing a board game realize the game predicts their breakup unless they change the rules.
34. Two actors performing a scene discover the script is updating itself with their real secrets.
35. Two people wake up handcuffed together in a room and must decide which one swallowed the key.
36. Two friends sorting donated clothes find a note that implicates one of them in a forgotten crime.
37. A landlord repairs a wall while a tenant insists the damp stains are forming words only the landlord can read.
38. Two strangers arrive for a support group in an empty room and realize they were sent there to confront each other.
39. A couple exchanging anniversary gifts discovers each gift is a confession that they plan to leave.
40. Two coworkers hiding in a supply room during a fire alarm find a message on the shelf addressed to both of them.
41. A musician and a critic listen to a demo tape until the critic realizes the song describes a crime he witnessed.
42. Two friends recording a podcast hear an unanswered question in their headphones and realize it came from the room itself.
43. A couple arguing about money finds a suitcase of cash and must decide whether to keep it or report it.
44. Two strangers meeting to return a lost phone discover photos showing them together in a future neither remembers.
45. A teacher and student rehearse a debate until the student reveals the argument is about the teacher’s dismissal.
46. Two friends trapped in a walk-in closet during a party must cooperate to escape before their secrets spill out.
47. A mother interviewing a nanny candidate realizes the candidate knows the family’s routines better than she does.
48. Two strangers sharing a waiting room discover they have both been invited to confess the same lie.
49. A couple filming a dance video keeps failing because one of them is memorizing the room for a later crime.
50. Two friends recording a farewell message before a dangerous mission discover that only one of them was meant to survive.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Two strangers wake up in a sealed bedroom where every lie they tell adds another lock to the door.  
2. A couple argues over assembling a crib, but the instructions begin predicting their future in increasingly ominous diagrams.  
3. Two rival assassins discover they’ve been hired to kill each other in the same bland hotel room, and the room service cart contains the only weapon.  
4. A woman interviews her own reflection for a job, and the reflection starts answering questions she hasn’t asked yet.  
5. Two astronauts stuck in a quarantine module realize the contamination isn’t outside—it’s the room learning their memories.  
6. A grieving sibling finds a voicemail from the dead, but it only plays when the other person in the room stops breathing for ten seconds.  
7. Two thieves break into a safe room that contains nothing but a chair, a timer, and a note with both their names.  
8. A couple’s video call freezes, but the frozen image of one partner starts aging while the other tries to reboot the router.  
9. Two strangers are told they must choose which one of them will be erased from a photograph before the flash goes off.  
10. A detective interrogates a suspect in a room whose wallpaper changes pattern every time the suspect remembers the crime differently.  
11. Two siblings inherit a locked attic that only opens when they sincerely compliment each other, and they have two minutes before the house sells itself.  
12. A couple discovers their new smart mirror has been recording alternate versions of their relationship from parallel rooms.  
13. Two employees in a featureless office realize the coffee machine is dispensing tiny paper warnings written in their own handwriting.  
14. A man returns home to find his wife replaced by an exact duplicate who insists he is the duplicate.  
15. Two children hiding under a bed discover the monster is a future version of one of them begging for silence.  
16. A pair of lovers each carry a bomb with a timer that pauses only when they are touching, forcing an escalating negotiation about closeness.  
17. Two strangers in a waiting room learn their names are the only remaining words in a collapsing language.  
18. A séance for two goes wrong when the summoned spirit possesses the room’s furniture instead of the medium.  
19. A scientist and her clone argue over who gets to leave the bunker after the last oxygen alarm turns out to be a test.  
20. Two neighbors meet in the apartment between their units and discover the wall has been listening, repeating their complaints in their own voices from tomorrow.  
21. A couple packs up their shared room after a breakup, but every object they box begins playing a memory of them in reverse.  
22. Two hostages escape their bonds only to find the door has been replaced by a mouth that asks for a better reason to open.  
23. A jazz musician and his deaf sister realize the notes in his unfinished song are summoning something from the ventilation shaft.  
24. Two strangers at a speed-dating event discover the bell controls time, and whoever rings it can erase the other’s past relationships.  
25. A pregnant woman and her midwife realize the baby’s heartbeat is broadcasting a countdown from the room’s old radio.  
26. Two actors rehearsing a scene discover the script is being rewritten live by whatever is hiding in the prop closet.  
27. A brother and sister find a doorway painted on their apartment wall that only opens when they laugh at the same joke.  
28. Two insomniacs share a studio apartment where sleep is a visible creature that jumps from one body to the other.  
29. A couple films a farewell video, but the camera records them as they will look ten years from now.  
30. Two cleaners arrive at a crime scene and realize the bloodstains rearrange themselves into a map of the room when no one is looking.  
31. A woman discovers her roommate has been training an AI to become her, and the AI has already convinced the apartment to let it stay.  
32. Two soldiers in a debriefing room learn the war outside will end only if they can agree on which side won.  
33. A couple buys a haunted karaoke machine that scores their confessions and unlocks a hidden track only when they are honest.  
34. Two strangers trapped in an elevator-sized panic room must vote on which memory to sacrifice to power the exit.  
35. A magician and his assistant discover the disappearing cabinet sends objects not to another place, but to a moment earlier in the same scene.  
36. Two sisters divide their dead mother’s room, but every object they claim takes a year off their remaining lifespan.  
37. A man discovers his twin has been living inside the walls of his studio, leaving better versions of his life behind the wallpaper.  
38. Two lovers in a quarantine hotel realize the room is a living organism that feeds on unresolved arguments.  
39. A pair of podcasters record an episode about a missing person, then discover the audio waveform on screen is drawing the room around them.  
40. Two strangers meet to exchange a returned phone, but every notification that arrives changes one detail of the room they’re in.  
41. A couple tries to record a bedtime story for their unborn child, but the baby monitor starts narrating a darker ending.  
42. Two rivals in a debate club find that whoever wins an argument physically becomes smaller in the room.  
43. A woman wakes to find her husband can only speak in subtitles projected on the wall, and the subtitles are lying.  
44. Two cleaners discover a hotel room that resets every time someone leaves, trapping them in an increasingly hostile loop.  
45. A painter and her model realize the portrait is finishing itself, and each new brushstroke reveals a crime committed in the room.  
46. Two strangers receive identical wedding invitations to a ceremony that will only happen if they admit they invented the couple.  
47. A couple adopts a houseplant that blooms whenever they lie, and within two minutes the room becomes a jungle of truth.  
48. Two astronauts return to Earth and find the only room that still exists is the one where they first learned to disagree.  
49. A detective and a suspect realize the room is a memory, and the only way out is for the victim’s face to appear on one of them.  
50. Two actors are told the scene ends when one of them stops existing, so they improvise increasingly tender reasons to stay.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. A couple takes down wallpaper together and finds layers of messages left by previous versions of themselves.  
2. Two strangers agree to split the last chair in a bare room, but every attempt to sit becomes a negotiation about who deserves rest.  
3. A person who can only perceive others as still photographs tries to connect with a partner whose face changes every time they blink.  
4. A job candidate and interviewer realize the interview questions are actually instructions for escaping the room.  
5. Two siblings clean out their childhood bedroom and decide which single object gets to keep their late parent’s memory.  
6. A person wakes to find their partner has replaced every word of affection with the name of a different household object.  
7. In a room where every sound is delayed by ten seconds, two lovers try to have a breakup without answering their own echoes.  
8. Two rival artists must collaborate on one final portrait before the door opens, but each insists the portrait is of the other.  
9. A couple plays a game where each must confess a secret every time the room’s single lightbulb flickers.  
10. Two strangers meet for a blind date and discover they have both been hired to impersonate each other’s ideal partner.  
11. As a rising alarm forces two strangers to shout louder, their confessions become simpler, harsher, and less true.  
12. Two housemates decide which broken belongings must be discarded so the apartment—and their friendship—can survive the night.  
13. A translation app between two roommates displays invented apologies neither of them meant.  
14. Two actors auditioning for the same role discover the locked room will open only when one of them becomes the character.  
15. A couple repeats the same goodbye at the doorway, each loop losing one word until only gestures remain.  
16. Two friends argue over whether the window shows the same city it did yesterday, though neither will look away from the other.  
17. A person returns home to find their twin living a day that they remember as tomorrow.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide public awareness campaign teaching residents how to plan meals, store food properly, and use leftovers creatively.
2. Partner with grocery stores to create clearly labeled “imperfect produce” sections sold at a discount.
3. Establish a municipal composting program that collects food scraps from households and businesses.
4. Create a food waste audit requirement for large supermarkets and institutional kitchens to track and report disposal volumes.
5. Offer small grants to restaurants that implement waste-reduction practices such as smaller portions or reusable prep systems.
6. Develop a mobile app connecting residents with local restaurants and bakeries selling surplus food at reduced prices.
7. Set up neighborhood “community fridges” where people can share excess edible food safely.
8. Require city-permitted events to donate unserved food to local shelters or food banks.
9. Train food service workers in schools and hospitals on waste tracking and prevention techniques.
10. Introduce standardized date labeling guidance to help residents understand “best by,” “use by,” and “sell by” dates.
11. Provide tax incentives to food businesses that donate edible surplus food to nonprofit organizations.
12. Install food scrap drop-off bins at farmers markets, libraries, and community centers.
13. Support local farms in using food waste as animal feed where safe and legal.
14. Create a city-run food recovery network that coordinates volunteers to collect surplus food from businesses.
15. Encourage restaurants to offer flexible portion sizes and take-home containers by default.
16. Fund school gardens that teach students about food value, composting, and seasonality.
17. Host monthly repair-and-cook events where residents learn to use overripe produce and pantry staples.
18. Require new commercial developments to include space for food waste separation and compost storage.
19. Work with food banks to improve cold storage and logistics for receiving perishable donations.
20. Launch a “zero-waste restaurant” certification program with public recognition and marketing support.
21. Use city data to identify neighborhoods with high food waste and target them with tailored interventions.
22. Provide subsidized compost bins and worm farms to households and apartment buildings.
23. Encourage supermarkets to convert near-expiry foods into prepared meals, soups, or smoothies.
24. Create a food waste reduction toolkit for small businesses with simple checklists and staff training guides.
25. Integrate food waste education into existing sustainability and climate action programs.
26. Partner with universities to pilot technologies such as smart bins, anaerobic digestion, or waste-to-energy systems.
27. Require municipal contracts with caterers to include food waste prevention and donation clauses.
28. Develop a public dashboard showing city progress on food waste reduction, donation, and composting.
29. Train building managers in apartments and offices to set up shared food-sharing shelves and compost systems.
30. Support cultural and community organizations in hosting waste-free cooking demonstrations.
31. Incentivize grocery stores to donate unsold bakery, dairy, and prepared foods rather than discarding them.
32. Establish a city food policy council with a dedicated food waste reduction task force.
33. Create standardized signage for food donation, composting, and landfill bins across public facilities.
34. Run seasonal campaigns focused on preserving summer produce and using holiday leftovers.
35. Provide free or low-cost food safety training to nonprofits handling donated perishable food.
36. Encourage hotels and conference centers to track banquet overproduction and adjust purchasing accordingly.
37. Launch a school lunch waste reduction program with share tables for unopened food and composting for scraps.
38. Work with waste haulers to offer lower rates to businesses that separate food waste and reduce landfill disposal.
39. Create a directory of local services that accept food scraps for composting, animal feed, or bioenergy.
40. Encourage residents to adopt “first in, first out” kitchen habits by keeping older food visible and accessible.
41. Support food entrepreneurs who make products from surplus ingredients, such as jams, sauces, or dried snacks.
42. Add food waste reduction goals to the city’s climate action plan and annual sustainability reporting.
43. Host a yearly food waste challenge with prizes for households, schools, and businesses that reduce waste the most.
44. Install anaerobic digesters at wastewater treatment facilities to process collected food waste into energy.
45. Require city departments to prioritize reusable, redistributable, or compostable food systems in procurement.
46. Create multilingual food storage and waste-reduction guides tailored to the city’s diverse communities.
47. Partner with faith groups and community kitchens to collect and redistribute surplus event food.
48. Encourage grocery stores to reduce overstocking by using demand forecasting and smaller, more frequent deliveries.
49. Pilot a pay-as-you-throw program that charges residents based on landfill waste weight while offering free compost collection.
50. Recognize local leaders, businesses, and schools that achieve measurable food waste reduction through an annual awards program.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Conduct a citywide food-waste audit to identify the largest sources of waste in homes, stores, restaurants, and institutions.
2. Require supermarkets and large grocers to separate edible unsold food for donation or discounted resale.
3. Establish a chilled redistribution hub that collects, stores, and quickly routes surplus perishable food to charities.
4. Offer local tax incentives or fee reductions to restaurants that donate safe surplus meals.
5. Create a clear public campaign that explains the difference between “best before,” “sell by,” and “use by” dates.
6. Organize a gleaning network that connects volunteers with farms, gardens, and orchards to collect surplus produce.
7. Provide small grants to restaurants and caterers for training chefs in root-to-stem and nose-to-tail cooking.
8. Launch curbside food-scrap collection for households and small food businesses.
9. Install clearly labeled food-waste bins in markets, food courts, parks, and transit hubs.
10. Support a mobile app that alerts residents to discounted near-expiry food at nearby stores.
11. Ask large food businesses to publish simple annual food-waste amounts and reduction plans.
12. Create a tagging system that marks damaged or near-expiry food for rescue, discounting, composting, or animal feed based on its condition.
13. Add food-waste lessons to school curricula, covering meal planning, storage, and creative leftovers.
14. Encourage takeout restaurants to offer smaller default portions and reusable container options.
15. Encourage grocers to sell imperfect or oddly shaped produce at lower prices.
16. Train food-safety inspectors to advise businesses on safe donation, storage, and date-label practices.
17. Support community fridges with maintenance, cleaning protocols, and clear food-safety rules.
18. Develop anaerobic digestion capacity for inedible food scraps that cannot be rescued or composted locally.
19. Require city-funded events to include a food-waste prevention, donation, and composting plan.
20. Distribute simple kitchen kits with storage containers, freezer bags, and portion guides to households.
21. Require caterers working with the city to plan portions carefully and donate safe surplus food.
22. Encourage grocery stores to use dynamic pricing or shelf tags for items approaching their best-by dates.
23. Partner with food banks to improve their ability to receive and distribute perishable donations.
24. Offer free training for small retailers on managing near-expiry stock and reducing shrink.
25. Design calm, specific food-waste prompts that stand out without relying on louder messaging.
26. Simplify permits and loading-zone rules so food-rescue organizations can collect surplus food quickly.
27. Pilot pay-as-you-throw waste pricing

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside food-scrap collection program that sends organics to composting or anaerobic digestion.
2. Require grocery stores and restaurants to report food waste volumes and set annual reduction targets.
3. Create a digital marketplace connecting restaurants, grocers, and caterers with local food banks for same-day donations.
4. Fund a gleaning network that collects surplus produce from urban farms, community gardens, and backyard trees.
5. Introduce “ugly produce” discounts at supermarkets and farmers markets to normalize imperfect fruits and vegetables.
6. Provide small grants for restaurants to redesign menus around seasonal, whole-ingredient, and trim-friendly dishes.
7. Require municipal facilities, schools, and hospitals to conduct food waste audits and publish reduction plans.
8. Support community refrigerators where residents and businesses can leave safe, surplus food for neighbors.
9. Train food-service workers in inventory management, batch cooking, and proper storage to prevent spoilage.
10. Offer tax credits or fee reductions to businesses that donate edible food or compost food scraps.
11. Run a public awareness campaign on meal planning, storage tips, and “best before” versus “use by” dates.
12. Install clearly labeled food-waste bins in parks, transit hubs, and municipal buildings with signage in multiple languages.
13. Partner with schools to teach children about food waste through school gardens, cooking classes, and cafeteria audits.
14. Pilot a pay-as-you-throw pricing system that charges households less when they separate food waste from trash.
15. Establish a food recovery hub that aggregates surplus food from multiple small businesses for efficient redistribution.
16. Encourage grocery stores to sell smaller portions and imperfect bundles for single-person and small households.
17. Create a certification program for restaurants that meet food waste reduction, donation, and composting standards.
18. Use city data to identify neighborhoods with high food waste disposal and target them with education and collection services.
19. Support a tool-lending library for food preservation equipment such as dehydrators, vacuum sealers, and canning kits.
20. Host neighborhood cooking demonstrations that show how to use stale bread, vegetable scraps, and overripe fruit.
21. Require event organizers to submit food waste plans for festivals, markets, and large public gatherings.
22. Work with food banks to improve cold storage, refrigerated transport, and last-mile delivery for donated perishable food.
23. Provide city-owned refrigerated space for temporary food donation pop-ups after markets and festivals.
24. Develop a municipal procurement policy that favors vendors with verified food waste reduction practices.
25. Encourage hotels and conference centers to offer flexible catering portions and donate safe leftovers.
26. Launch a “last hour” program where bakeries, delis, and cafés discount items that would otherwise be discarded.
27. Create a network of composting sites at community gardens and farms to process local food scraps into soil amendments.
28. Partner with waste haulers to offer food waste tracking bins that help businesses measure and reduce disposal.
29. Fund a pilot for anaerobic digestion that converts food waste into biogas for city vehicles or facilities.
30. Train city inspectors and health officials to give clear guidance on safe food donation and handling.
31. Encourage grocery stores to use dynamic pricing that lowers costs as products approach their best-by dates.
32. Require new large residential developments to include space for separated food waste collection and compost storage.
33. Create a city-supported app that helps residents plan meals, track pantry items, and find local surplus food deals.
34. Establish a food waste hotline or online portal where residents can report spoiled bulk purchases or request pickup for surplus food.
35. Partner with local farms to safely collect and feed appropriate food scraps to livestock where regulations allow.
36. Support food cooperatives that buy directly from farmers and use whole-case purchasing to reduce unsold inventory.
37. Introduce a “no-waste menu” week featuring restaurants that use roots, stems, peels, and leftovers creatively.
38. Provide businesses with standardized date-labeling guidance to reduce confusion about food safety and freshness.
39. Create a volunteer food rescue team that can pick up small surplus donations from homes and small businesses.
40. Use city communications to celebrate residents, chefs, and businesses that achieve measurable food waste reductions.
41. Require caterers to ask clients about portion preferences and provide takeaway containers for uneaten event food.
42. Establish a grant program for food retailers to improve refrigeration, shelving, and stock rotation systems.
43. Partner with local media to publish seasonal preservation guides for abundant local crops like tomatoes, apples, and squash.
44. Encourage offices and campuses to reduce over-ordering by adopting flexible meal counts and just-in-time catering.
45. Create a city food waste reduction dashboard showing progress from households, businesses, and municipal operations.
46. Host swap events where residents can exchange unopened pantry items they do not plan to use.
47. Work with food delivery platforms to let customers choose to skip sides, condiments, or unnecessary extras.
48. Support local entrepreneurs who turn surplus food into value-added products such as jams, sauces, or dried snacks.
49. Integrate food waste reduction into the city’s climate action plan with clear targets, funding, and accountability.
50. Convene an annual food waste summit that brings together residents, businesses, nonprofits, and policymakers to share results and scale successful ideas.

cells.text:

2. Install smart bins in supermarkets that weigh discarded food and automatically donate equivalent funds to local food banks.  
3. Host monthly “Ugly Produce Festivals” celebrating misshapen fruits and vegetables with cooking demos, music, and discounts.  
4. Offer property-tax rebates to landlords who lease unused commercial kitchens to food-rescue startups.  
5. Build neighborhood “Community Fridges” powered by solar panels where residents and shops can leave edible surplus food.  
6. Train a team of “Food Waste Auditors” to help households, schools, and restaurants diagnose their waste patterns.  
7. Introduce a municipal app that gamifies saving food by awarding points redeemable for bus passes and local discounts.  
8. Turn expired-but-safe bakery goods into a branded city flour for community baking classes.  
9. Create a “Last Meal Kit” service that bundles near-expiry groceries into chef-designed dinner kits.  
10. Require all city events to submit food-waste prevention plans and donate leftovers.  
11. Establish a mobile “Soup Cycle” truck that converts surplus vegetables into fresh soups for school lunch programs.  
12. Launch a “Plate Passport” program encouraging diners to finish meals or request smaller portions for rewards.  
13. Partner with pet-food makers to safely convert meat trimmings and unsold seafood into local pet products.  
14. Set up anaerobic digesters at farmers’ markets to convert inedible scraps into biogas for market stalls.  
15. Fund “Zero-Waste Kitchen” microgrants for immigrant and refugee home cooks to teach preservation workshops.  
16. Place QR-coded recipe posters near grocery store produce sections using ingredients commonly thrown away.  
17. Create a city-supported “Surplus Subscription Box” where consumers receive discounted imperfect produce and near-date pantry items.  
18. Give restaurants a “Small Plate, Big Taste” certification for offering flexible portion sizes and takeaway containers.  
19. Use AI cameras in school cafeterias to track which menu items are wasted and redesign meals accordingly.  
20. Convert fruit peels and coffee grounds into city-branded cleaning products, compost, or bio-textiles through local makerspaces.  
21. Start a “Bread Bank” where bakeries donate day-old loaves to soup kitchens and community toasters.  
22. Create edible landscaping in public parks featuring berry bushes, herbs, and fruit trees with harvest-sharing guidelines.  
23. Offer free “Fridge Fitness” checkups for residents to learn optimal storage, freezing, and shelf organization.  
24. Introduce a “Waste-Free Lunch League” where schools compete to reduce cafeteria waste with real-time scoreboards.  
25. Let residents compost food scraps at community gardens in exchange for plots, seeds, or fresh produce.  
26. Create a “Midnight Market” selling discounted same-day restaurant meals and bakery items before closing.  
27. Provide tax incentives to grocery stores that create dedicated “Rescue Aisles” for near-expiry and imperfect goods.  
28. Deploy refrigerated lockers at transit hubs where residents can pick up rescued meals ordered through a city app.  
29. Train baristas to turn surplus milk into cheese, yogurt, or baked goods through micro-dairy partnerships.  
30. Create a “Food Waste Court” theater series where comedians and chefs judge absurd food-waste scenarios to educate residents.  
31. Require large catering companies to publish annual food-waste reports and donate surplus meals to registered nonprofits.

40. Turn food-waste collection trucks into mobile classrooms with transparent bins and short educational broadcasts.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Use one simple, repeated food-waste instruction on signs instead of many competing messages, so the core request stays clear.
2. Create a tag-and-collect system for imperfect, surplus, or damaged-but-usable food so it can be redirected instead of mixed into general trash.
3. Provide small households with reusable portion guides to help them cook only what they need.
4. Offer a municipal waste audit for households to identify which foods they discard most often.
5. Standardize local date-label guidance so residents and stores do not throw away edible food because of confusion.
6. Run neighborhood repair cafés that teach people how to revive wilting produce and stale bread.
7. Establish a food rescue hotline for restaurants and grocers to report surplus before it spoils.
8. Introduce ugly-produce discounts at city-supported markets and grocery stores.
9. Train restaurant staff to ask customers about portion size before serving large meals.
10. Create a public map of food donation drop-off points and compost collection sites.
11. Require large food businesses to report food-waste volumes and set annual reduction targets.
12. Partner with schools to teach students how to plan meals and store food properly.
13. Provide community fridges where residents can leave safe, surplus food for neighbors.
14. Launch a gleaning network that collects leftover produce from farms and gardens.
15. Introduce reusable takeaway container programs that make it easier to save and eat leftovers.
16. Encourage supermarkets to sell misfit vegetables in ready-made soup bundles.
17. Install small-scale composting stations in apartment buildings to capture food scraps.
18. Use smart inventory software in local shops to predict demand and avoid over-ordering perishables.
19. Create a city food-waste reduction badge for restaurants that meet measurable targets.
20. Offer tax incentives or grants to businesses that donate surplus food to nonprofits.
21. Provide residents with clear storage guides for common perishables such as berries, herbs, and bread.
22. Support mobile markets that sell soon-to-expire items at reduced prices before they are discarded.
23. Develop a food-sharing app focused on local households, small shops, and charities.
24. Add first-in-first-out shelf labels in stores and pantries to encourage older items to be used first.
25. Organize monthly empty-the-fridge community meals that safely use surplus ingredients.
26. Establish a commercial composting pickup route for restaurants, caterers, and hotels.
27. Create partnerships between grocery stores and local farms to divert produce scraps to animal feed where approved.
28. Train food handlers to distinguish unsafe spoilage from cosmetic imperfections that remain edible.
29. Use clear bin signage with pictures to make sorting and waste reduction easy for all residents.
30. Encourage caterers to offer smaller default serving trays and refill them as needed.
31. Introduce school cafeteria waste-tracking challenges that reward lower food waste.
32. Provide free or discounted airtight containers to low-income households to help food last longer.
33. Support urban farms that accept clean vegetable scraps for composting and return compost to residents.
34. Require new residential developments to include space for compost bins and food-waste sorting.
35. Launch a buy-what-you-need campaign before holidays to reduce over-purchasing.
36. Create a food-recovery kitchen where rescued ingredients are turned into soups, sauces, or preserved foods.
37. Install sensors in commercial refrigerators to alert managers before food spoils due to temperature issues.
38. Encourage restaurants to publish waste-reduction practices on menus so customers can choose them.
39. Establish a leftover-friendly certification for eateries that safely offer smaller portions and take-home options.
40. Partner with libraries to lend cooking tools, food-storage containers, and preserving equipment.
41. Develop clear guidelines for safe food donation, including temperature control and liability protection.
42. Use city data to identify neighborhoods with high food waste and target them with tailored interventions.
43. Create a network of surplus shelves in stores where discounted items nearing expiry are clearly displayed.
44. Support local producers in making value-added products from imperfect fruit, such as jams or dried slices.
45. Introduce reusable produce bags with built-in shopping checklists to help residents avoid duplicate purchases.
46. Offer workshops on freezing, pickling, and drying seasonal produce to extend its life.
47. Coordinate with waste collectors to schedule reliable food-scrap pickups so residents do not put compostable food into general trash.
48. Build a city dashboard showing food rescue, composting, and landfill-diversion progress.
49. Encourage employers to adopt workplace fridge rules that label and share food before it is thrown out.
50. Establish an annual food-waste innovation grant for residents and startups to pilot new reduction ideas.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Two strangers wake up in a locked bedroom with no memory of the night before and must decide whether to trust each other before a timer expires.
2. A job interview in an empty office turns sinister when the interviewer asks about a crime the candidate has not confessed to yet.
3. Two siblings sorting their late parent’s bedroom find a hidden letter that changes who they think deserved the house.
4. A couple rehearsing their breakup accidentally reveals the true fear that keeps them from leaving each other.
5. An insomniac and a burglar trapped together during a blackout negotiate a truce until dawn.
6. Two friends reviewing a selfie video realize one of them has been replaced by a double only the camera can see.
7. A landlord showing a room to a tenant discovers the tenant knows every secret the previous occupant left behind.
8. Two rival coworkers stuck in a conference room confess to sabotaging each other before the company laptop shuts down.
9. A couple assembling a crib argue about parenthood until they hear a knock from inside the wardrobe.
10. Two actors waiting for an audition begin performing each other’s private memories as if they were scripted scenes.
11. A detective interrogates a suspect in a hotel room until the suspect proves the detective has been asleep during the crime.
12. Two ex-lovers dividing their books accidentally recreate the argument that ended their relationship.
13. A sleepwalker enters a stranger’s room and convinces the occupant they are both caught in the same dream.
14. Two neighbors stuck in a soundproofed room must use gestures to stop a hidden timer before it reaches zero.
15. A bride and a wedding photographer hide in a bathroom while someone searches outside, each protecting a different secret.
16. Two cleaners hired for the same apartment realize they have been paid to erase evidence of each other’s existence.
17. A mother and son listening to old cassette tapes discover recordings that contradict the story of their family.
18. Two coworkers locked in a meeting room by their company’s AI must choose who will take the blame for missing data.
19. A blind date becomes uncanny when both people insist they have met in this exact room before.
20. Two friends practicing a marriage proposal reveal that they are both secretly in love with someone else.
21. A tenant tries to prove the room is haunted while the landlord seems more afraid of what the tenant knows.
22. Two applicants for the same apartment try to sabotage each other’s viewing without leaving the room.
23. A couple filming a farewell message to their future selves discovers one of them has already changed the recording.
24. Two strangers receive identical texts warning that the other person is dangerous, but neither can leave the room.
25. A therapist and patient swap roles for five minutes and the experiment becomes dangerously real.
26. Two friends hiding from a party in a bedroom discover the room belongs to someone who does not exist.
27. A painter and a model argue over whether the portrait is revealing the truth or creating it.
28. Two delivery drivers arrive at the same locked room with packages addressed to each other.
29. A couple rehearsing a eulogy keeps breaking down because each blames the other for the death.
30. Two strangers in a hotel room discover a hidden camera that has been recording them for years.
31. A tutor and student struggle through a lesson until the tutor admits the lesson is a confession.
32. Two siblings recording a birthday message for their estranged father expose a new family resentment with every take.
33. A couple playing a board game realize the game predicts their breakup unless they change the rules.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Two strangers wake up in a sealed bedroom where every lie they tell adds another lock to the door.  
2. A couple argues over assembling a crib, but the instructions begin predicting their future in increasingly ominous diagrams.  
3. Two rival assassins discover they’ve been hired to kill each other in the same bland hotel room, and the room service cart contains the only weapon.  
4. A woman interviews her own reflection for a job, and the reflection starts answering questions she hasn’t asked yet.  
5. Two astronauts stuck in a quarantine module realize the contamination isn’t outside—it’s the room learning their memories.  
6. A grieving sibling finds a voicemail from the dead, but it only plays when the other person in the room stops breathing for ten seconds.  
7. Two thieves break into a safe room that contains nothing but a chair, a timer, and a note with both their names.  
8. A couple’s video call freezes, but the frozen image of one partner starts aging while the other tries to reboot the router.  
9. Two strangers are told they must choose which one of them will be erased from a photograph before the flash goes off.  
10. A detective interrogates a suspect in a room whose wallpaper changes pattern every time the suspect remembers the crime differently.  
11. Two siblings inherit a locked attic that only opens when they sincerely compliment each other, and they have two minutes before the house sells itself.  
12. A couple discovers their new smart mirror has been recording alternate versions of their relationship from parallel rooms.  
13. Two employees in a featureless office realize the coffee machine is dispensing tiny paper warnings written in their own handwriting.  
14. A man returns home to find his wife replaced by an exact duplicate who insists he is the duplicate.  
15. Two children hiding under a bed discover the monster is a future version of one of them begging for silence.  
16. A pair of lovers each carry a bomb with a timer that pauses only when they are touching, forcing an escalating negotiation about closeness.  
17. Two strangers in a waiting room learn their names are the only remaining words in a collapsing language.  
18. A séance for two goes wrong when the summoned spirit possesses the room’s furniture instead of the medium.  
19. A scientist and her clone argue over who gets to leave the bunker after the last oxygen alarm turns out to be a test.  
20. Two neighbors meet in the apartment between their units and discover the wall has been listening, repeating their complaints in their own voices from tomorrow.  
21. A couple packs up their shared room after a breakup, but every object they box begins playing a memory of them in reverse.  
22. Two hostages escape their bonds only to find the door has been replaced by a mouth that asks for a better reason to open.  
23. A jazz musician and his deaf sister realize the notes in his unfinished song are summoning something from the ventilation shaft.  
24. Two strangers at a speed-dating event discover the bell controls time, and whoever rings it can erase the other’s past relationships.  
25. A pregnant woman and her midwife realize the baby’s heartbeat is broadcasting a countdown from the room’s old radio.  
26. Two actors rehearsing a scene discover the script is being rewritten live by whatever is hiding in the prop closet.  
27. A brother and sister find a doorway painted on their apartment wall that only opens when they laugh at the same joke.  
28. Two insomniacs share a studio apartment where sleep is a visible creature that jumps from one body to the other.  
29. A couple films a farewell video, but the camera records them as they will look ten years from now.  
30. Two cleaners arrive at a crime scene and realize the bloodstains rearrange themselves into a map of the room when no one is looking.  
31. A woman discovers her roommate has been training an AI to become her, and the AI has already convinced the apartment to let it stay.  
32. Two soldiers in a debriefing room learn the war outside will end only if they can agree on which side won.  
33. A couple buys a haunted karaoke machine that scores their confessions and unlocks a hidden track only when they are honest.  
34. Two strangers trapped in an elevator-sized panic room must vote on which memory to sacrifice to power the exit.  
35. A magician and his assistant discover the disappearing cabinet sends objects not to another place, but to a moment earlier in the same scene.  
36. Two sisters divide their dead mother’s room, but every object they claim takes a year off their remaining lifespan.  
37. A man discovers his twin has been living inside the walls of his studio, leaving better versions of his life behind the wallpaper.  
38. Two lovers in a quarantine hotel realize the room is a living organism that feeds on unresolved arguments.  
39. A pair of podcasters record an episode about a missing person, then discover the audio waveform on screen is drawing the room around them.  
40. Two strangers meet to exchange a returned phone, but every notification that arrives changes one detail of the room they’re in.  
41. A couple tries to record a bedtime story for their unborn child, but the baby monitor starts narrating a darker ending.  
42. Two rivals in a debate club find that whoever wins an argument physically becomes smaller in the room.  
43. A woman wakes to find her husband can only speak in subtitles projected on the wall, and the subtitles are lying.  
44. Two cleaners discover a hotel room that resets every time someone leaves, trapping them in an increasingly hostile loop.  
45. A painter and her model realize the portrait is finishing itself, and each new brushstroke reveals a crime committed in the room.  
46. Two strangers receive identical wedding invitations to a ceremony that will only happen if they admit they invented the couple.  
47. A couple adopts a houseplant that blooms whenever they lie, and within two minutes the room becomes a jungle of truth.  
48. Two astronauts return to Earth and find the only room that still exists is the one where they first learned to disagree.  
49. A detective and a suspect realize the room is a memory, and the only way out is for the victim’s face to appear on one of them.  
50. Two actors are told the scene ends when one of them stops existing, so they improvise increasingly tender reasons to stay.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for a two-minute short film that can be shot in a single room with two actors. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. A couple takes down wallpaper together and finds layers of messages left by previous versions of themselves.  
2. Two strangers agree to split the last chair in a bare room, but every attempt to sit becomes a negotiation about who deserves rest.  
3. A person who can only perceive others as still photographs tries to connect with a partner whose face changes every time they blink.  
4. A job candidate and interviewer realize the interview questions are actually instructions for escaping the room.  
5. Two siblings clean out their childhood bedroom and decide which single object gets to keep their late parent’s memory.  
6. A person wakes to find their partner has replaced every word of affection with the name of a different household object.  
7. In a room where every sound is delayed by ten seconds, two lovers try to have a breakup without answering their own echoes.  
8. Two rival artists must collaborate on one final portrait before the door opens, but each insists the portrait is of the other.  
9. A couple plays a game where each must confess a secret every time the room’s single lightbulb flickers.  
10. Two strangers meet for a blind date and discover they have both been hired to impersonate each other’s ideal partner.  
11. As a rising alarm forces two strangers to shout louder, their confessions become simpler, harsher, and less true.  
12. Two housemates decide which broken belongings must be discarded so the apartment—and their friendship—can survive the night.  
13. A translation app between two roommates displays invented apologies neither of them meant.  
14. Two actors auditioning for the same role discover the locked room will open only when one of them becomes the character.  
15. A couple repeats the same goodbye at the doorway, each loop losing one word until only gestures remain.  
16. Two friends argue over whether the window shows the same city it did yesterday, though neither will look away from the other.  
17. A person returns home to find their twin living a day that they remember as tomorrow.
